title: Robotics Foundations
tagline: How any robot senses, thinks and acts, explained with no jargon.
description: Learn how robots work with no jargon. Ten short story-based lessons on sensors, motors, walking and learning.
outcome: After this course you can explain how a robot works, name its main parts, and describe how it learns.
whoFor: Curious beginners, students from about age 12, parents and teachers who want a gentle first look at robotics.
prerequisites: None. No maths or coding needed.
outcomes: Explain how a robot senses, thinks and acts
Name the main kinds of robots and what each is good at
Describe how sensors and motors work
Explain, in simple words, how robots walk and learn
Describe where robots really work today

finalActivity.title: Choose a small job for a robot
finalActivity.prompt: Choose a small job for a robot and write it in one sentence. Then say what it must sense, what it must decide and what it must do.

lessons.title: Before Robots
lessons.summary: Explain how a self-opening temple door shows the idea of a machine acting on its own.

quiz.q: What makes a self-opening door an early example of a machine acting on its own?
options: A person pulls it open by hand
A hidden mechanism reacts and opens it without anyone pushing
quiz.why: Such doors used a mechanism (heat, steam or weights) so the door moved by itself.

quiz.q: The big idea behind a robot is a machine that…
options: Does a job without a person controlling every step
quiz.why: Acting on its own, without step-by-step human control, is the core idea.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT needed for a machine to act on its own?
quiz.why: A face is optional; a trigger and a way to move are what matter.

quiz.q: Why do people study old machines when learning robotics?
options: They show ideas that modern robots still use
quiz.why: Many robot ideas, like reacting to the world, started long ago.

lessons.title: From Rules to Robots at Work
lessons.summary: Describe what the first industrial robot arm did and why it mattered.

quiz.q: What did the first industrial robot arm mostly do?
options: Repeat a dull, heavy or dangerous job in a factory
quiz.why: Early industrial arms lifted and moved parts in factories.

quiz.q: Why was it useful to let a robot arm do dangerous factory jobs?
options: It removed the need for electricity
It kept people away from harm
quiz.why: Moving danger from people to machines was a major benefit.

quiz.q: An early robot arm followed…
options: Instructions shouted from across the room
A fixed list of stored steps
quiz.why: It replayed steps it had been taught, over and over.

quiz.q: What was the main limit of those first arms?
options: They were too slow to be used
They could not cope when the job changed unexpectedly
quiz.why: Fixed rules work only while the situation stays the same.

lessons.title: Kinds of Robots
lessons.summary: Group robots by how they move: rolling, walking, flying and fixed.

quiz.q: A robot vacuum belongs to which group?
quiz.why: It moves on wheels, so it is a rolling robot.

quiz.q: A factory robot arm bolted to the floor is…
quiz.why: It stays in one place and reaches around, so it is a fixed robot.

quiz.q: Which robot group is usually best for looking at a large field from above?
quiz.why: Drones see wide areas from the air.

quiz.q: Why might a designer choose a walking robot over a rolling one?
options: It can cross stairs and rough ground
quiz.why: Legs can step over obstacles that wheels cannot.

lessons.title: How Robots Sense
lessons.summary: Explain what sensors do and name a few kinds.

quiz.q: What does a sensor do?
options: Turns something in the world into a signal the robot can use
quiz.why: Sensors measure things like light, distance or touch.

quiz.q: Which sensor helps a robot judge how far away a wall is?
quiz.why: A distance sensor measures how far an object is.

quiz.q: A camera helps a robot mainly to…
quiz.why: A camera captures images.

quiz.q: Why do many robots use more than one kind of sensor?
options: Each sensor has things it cannot measure
Robots are required to by law
quiz.why: Different sensors cover each other's blind spots.

lessons.title: How a Robot Thinks
lessons.summary: Describe the sense-think-act loop using a robot vacuum.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of the loop?
quiz.why: A robot senses, decides, then acts, again and again.

quiz.q: A robot vacuum bumps into a chair leg. Which step is that?
quiz.why: The bump is the robot sensing something.

quiz.q: After sensing the chair, the vacuum turns away. Turning is the…
quiz.why: Turning is the action that follows the decision.

quiz.q: Why does the loop keep repeating?
options: The world keeps changing, so the robot keeps checking
quiz.why: Repeating lets the robot correct itself as things change.

lessons.title: How a Robot Acts
lessons.summary: Explain how motors turn a decision into movement.

quiz.q: What turns a robot's decision into movement?
quiz.why: Actuators such as motors create motion.

quiz.q: A motor mainly changes electrical energy into…
quiz.why: Electric motors turn electricity into spinning motion.

quiz.q: What can a gear do for a motor?
quiz.why: Gears can give more turning force at lower speed.

quiz.q: If a robot makes a decision but has no actuator, what happens?
quiz.why: Without an actuator the decision cannot become movement.

lessons.title: How Robots Walk
lessons.summary: Explain why walking is harder than rolling and how balance is kept.

quiz.q: Why is walking harder than rolling for a robot?
options: Legs are always heavier than wheels
It must keep balance while each foot lifts
quiz.why: A walking robot is constantly at risk of falling over.

quiz.q: Which sensor helps a walking robot know if it is tilting?
quiz.why: Balance sensors tell the robot how it is leaning.

quiz.q: When a walking robot starts to lean, it should…
options: Move a foot or shift weight to stay up
quiz.why: Constant small corrections keep a robot upright.

quiz.q: Why are wheels often chosen when the floor is flat and smooth?
quiz.why: On smooth floors wheels are simple and stable.

lessons.title: How Robots Learn
lessons.summary: Explain learning from practice instead of writing a rule for every case.

quiz.q: What is the idea behind a robot learning from practice?
options: It improves by trying and seeing what works
A person writes every rule in advance
quiz.why: Learning means improving from experience.

quiz.q: Why not just write a rule for every case?
options: There are far too many cases to list
quiz.why: The real world has too many situations to cover with hand-written rules.

quiz.q: In practice learning, a good result usually earns…
options: A reward that tells the robot it did well
quiz.why: Rewards guide the robot toward better choices.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a robot learning?
options: It gets better at grasping after many tries
It follows one fixed script forever
It switches off to save power
quiz.why: Getting better with tries is learning.

lessons.title: Robots at Work
lessons.summary: Describe where robots help people in factories, farms and hospitals.

quiz.q: A common robot job in factories is…
quiz.why: Factories use robots for repeated, precise work.

quiz.q: How can robots help on farms?
quiz.why: Farm robots help with crop care and harvesting.

quiz.q: In hospitals, robots can help by…
quiz.why: Surgical robots help doctors, they do not replace them.

quiz.q: What do many robot jobs have in common?
options: They are repeated, precise or risky for people
quiz.why: Robots shine where jobs are repeated, exact or dangerous.

lessons.title: The Future and Your First Robot
lessons.summary: Recognise the main parts that go into building a small robot.

quiz.q: Which part acts as a small robot's brain?
quiz.why: A control board runs the program and makes decisions.

quiz.q: Which parts let a small robot move?
quiz.why: Motors with wheels move a rolling robot.

quiz.q: A small robot needs power. What supplies it?
quiz.why: Batteries store the energy a robot uses.

quiz.q: A first small robot should do…
quiz.why: Start with one small, clear job.
